UNDER THE HOOD

Nine approaches.
Different tradeoffs.

01 / FOLLOW

Hamiltonian cycle

Follow a closed route through every cell. Simple, predictable, and our reference for move counts.

02 / SHORTEN

Safe shortcuts

Skip forward toward food while preserving body order. Account for the moving tail and growth on every move.

03 / REWIRE

Dynamic repair

Split and reconnect the cycle around squares, accepting only safe changes that shorten the food route. Then use shortcuts.

04 / PLAN

Compact planner

Keep every body edge on the cycle. Search alternative routes through the empty area, then replan as the tail moves.

05 / CERTIFY

Certified routes

Simulate a shorter route to food, then prove the resulting body fits a full-board cycle. Only take the route after both checks pass.

06 / SWITCH

Greedy → certified

Chase food with simulated routes and tail-access checks. At the selected occupancy, seek a verified cycle and switch to Certified routes. The early phase is experimental, with no full-game guarantee.

07 / EXPAND

Adaptive partial loops

Take routes ending on smaller loops. Keep checked connections to every omitted region, and expand when the tail clears a bridge. Score shortcuts against the cost of reaching the next food.

08 / COMBINE

Greedy → partial loops

Chase food with local safety checks, then hand off to checked partial loops near the selected occupancy. The early phase is experimental; the expansion certificate is required before switching.

09 / FLEX

Flexible certificates

Drive on the right inside 2×2 blocks, so every cell has two moves and the body grows as a tree of blocks. Before every move, build and check a full-board cycle for the new position. Look one imagined apple ahead to pick between the two moves. Guaranteed from the first move.

Safety, reproducibility, and what these numbers mean +

Completion of the first five: These solvers use obstacle-free, even-sized boards, one food at a time, and growth by one cell. Ordered body positions preserve a safe next move. The first four solvers reduce forward cycle distance on every move. Certified routes instead count remaining steps in the committed route while temporarily off-cycle; a compatible cycle is restored at food. This prevents an endless survival loop.

Fair comparison: Each solver receives the same seeded random numbers and selects food uniformly from its own free cells in row-major order. Food coordinates can diverge because the snakes occupy different cells. Batch averages are more useful than the winner of one seed.

Dynamic repair: At most two improving passes per move, each considering up to 48 possible first square flips. Reconsider newly available repairs immediately as the tail moves. A second flip reconnects the split loops. The full cycle and body order are checked before acceptance. This is a bounded heuristic, not an optimal solver.

Compact planner: Locks all body edges, keeping every empty cell in the forward arc between head and tail. It searches improving paired square flips and, once per food, explores 512 candidate changes with a separate seeded random stream. Up to eight improving passes run every move, so newly unlocked tail edges are considered immediately. Temporary detours stay inside the search; the live game accepts only shorter routes and follows the cycle. More computation buys fewer moves on average, not a proven optimum.

Certified routes: Tries clear routes and bounded searches over the moving body, simulates tail movement and growth, then searches for a Hamiltonian cycle containing the resulting body (up to 2,000 search nodes per candidate). A route must be strictly shorter than the current safe route. During play, replace it only with a strictly shorter route carrying a newly verified certificate; otherwise retain the existing plan. Without an active route, search again every move; a failed or unfinished search leaves the compact fallback in place. During a committed route, the overlay shows the future cycle certificate and a dashed white line shows the remaining route. Full-board winning routes need no further certificate.

Hybrid: No full-board cycle is required for early food routes. Search with tail movement included, simulate the whole route, and check tail access after eating. Among equal-length food routes, prefer the resulting body with better access to possible next food cells. Recheck the route every move: accept a shorter safe route, or an equally short route with a better exit. Use a stretched head-to-tail escape path when needed. Before crossing the selected occupancy target, try to certify the resulting body, or certify the current body during recovery. A failed search never installs an incompatible cycle. The actual handoff can be earlier by one cell or later than the target; the card reports the actual length. Local checks do not prove eventual completion. A finite move budget stops looping runs, which count as incomplete in benchmarks. The cycle overlay is hidden during uncertified early play; dashed lines show committed routes.

Adaptive partial loops: Short food routes end on a checked loop containing the body. Other cells form empty loops with recorded merges. The solver clears a connection with the tail before restoring the next region. It also trims its current loop when savings outweigh estimated recovery costs. The overlay shows the terminal local loop during a food route. A local loop alone is insufficient: the full expansion record is checked. This solver has a larger proven move bound than the first five; compare actual moves as well as completion.

Greedy → partial loops: Uses the same early greedy routing as approach 6, but switches to a partial-loop expansion certificate instead of requiring a Hamiltonian cycle immediately. The shared greedy switch control applies to approaches 6 and 8. The greedy phase has no completion guarantee. Unchecked algorithms do not advance or plan; selection also limits benchmark workers.

Flexible certificates: The board is split into 2×2 blocks and the snake keeps right inside each block, so every cell has only two legal moves. The blocks the snake has visited form a tree, and the outline of a tree of blocks is a cycle through every cell. Before every move, the solver builds that cycle for the position after the move and checks it cell by cell: the body must lie on it as one unbroken stretch with all free cells ahead of the head. If no move toward food passes, the snake follows its current cycle, which is always safe. Each food gets a budget of free moves; after that, a move is taken only if it brings the food strictly closer along the new cycle, so the snake cannot circle forever. To choose between its two moves, it searches up to 3,000 positions for the fewest moves to the current food, then adds the cost of 12 imagined next foods spread evenly along the cycle. The imagined foods use their own random stream and never read the real next food. Boards with an odd side have no 2×2 blocks: there it plans a free route and takes it only if a safe cycle is proven for the moment of eating. Unlike approaches 6 and 8, there is no unguaranteed phase. The idea of keep-right routing inside 2×2 blocks comes from twanvl/snake (MIT licence); the per-move certificate, progress budget, and look-ahead are new here.

Metrics: A move is one grid-cell step. “vs. cycle” is the reduction in mean moves, not a gap to a known optimum. Compute time includes simulation and planning, excludes animation, and depends on your device. Move averages include completed games only; failures are shown separately.

Background tabs: Playback includes a 5 moves/second mode. Expand later six hides the first three algorithms. Click a board to focus it; Escape or Back to comparison restores the grid. Playback controls, including restart and Back, affect only visible algorithms; hidden games retain their state and stay paused. Each algorithm has its own rewind history. Back (or Left Arrow) pauses and rewinds one recorded step per visible algorithm, restoring its body, food, routes, counters, and chart. Step (or Right Arrow) replays recorded decisions exactly. Restart clears visible histories; changing board/seed/hybrid target resets all nine games and histories. Switching views preserves them. Animation may pause when the tab is hidden. Benchmark computation uses a separate worker. The CSV includes each seed, board size, result, move count, shortcut count, repair count, compute time, the hybrid target and actual handoff, and route-revision counts.
